implementation_notes: Ruby states are plain objects: the context keeps @state, forwards state-dependent calls and assigns a successor to transition; there is no interface to declare, so duck typing replaces the State abstraction and the state objects are replaced by whatever class or singleton implements the operations. Because Ruby ships Delegator/SimpleDelegator and Forwardable, a context can delegate whole method sets to the current state instead of hand-writing forwarding methods, while method_missing can forward everything at the price of hiding the real owner from tracebacks and respond_to?. Gem-based machines (AASM and friends) are the library route when transitions must integrate with ActiveRecord callbacks and validations.
code_sketch:
class Draft
  def publish(doc)
    doc.state = Published.new
  end
end

class Document
  attr_accessor :state                 # transitions assign through this writer
  def initialize = @state = Draft.new
  def publish = state.publish(self)    # states are plain objects
end
pitfalls: attr_accessor makes the transition writable from anywhere; expose a narrow transition_to method instead.
SimpleDelegator and method_missing hide the real receiver from stack traces, respond_to? and documentation - Forwardable#def_delegators keeps the surface explicit.
State objects shared as constants must be frozen and must not memoize per-document values.
